quoted_clause: 68% of requests terminating in T=1, 25% in T=2, 5% in T=3, and 2% exceeding the turn limit (falling back to single-shot). That makes ... the 95th percentile T=3 (cumulative 68+25+5 = 98% by T=3).
observed: The fallback population is counted inconsistently. If the 2% exceeding the turn limit fall back to single-shot, they are T=1, so the distribution becomes 70% T=1, 25% T=2, 5% T=3; cumulative at T=2 is 95%, making p95 T=2, not T=3. If the 2% are excluded, p95=T=3 only for the successful-request subpopulation, not for all requests.
evidence: Fallback T=1: 68+2=70% at T=1; 70+25=95% by T=2; p95=T=2. At T=2, I=9,200+2×865+300=11,230 tokens; KV=11,230×2.62144 MB≈29.43 GB; C=436/29.43≈14.8, floor 14, not the printed 13.8/floor 13. Excluding fallback: p95 of successful requests is T=3, but overall p95 including fallback T=1 is T=2.
root_cause: Population/denominator error: fallback requests are assigned to a separate tail while also being described as single-shot, and the percentile is computed on the wrong population.
correction: Define explicitly whether fallback requests are T=1 or excluded. If T=1, p95=T=2 and update C≈14.8 (floor 14) and all downstream agentic host counts. If excluded, label the percentile as 'among successful requests' and carry the 2% fallback/failure rate separately. Recompute all T=3 stress-point numbers.
acceptance_test: The turn distribution sums to 100% with fallback assigned; p95 is recomputed from that distribution; downstream C, W, and host counts are updated and consistent.

quoted_clause: Sizing at the 25 ms budget is a tighter internal target than the 40 ms SLO pole, so name the sizing pole once and state it once: sizing at the SLO pole gives ~31 hosts
observed: The ~31-host figure is a full-utilization KV screen (523/17≈30.8), not the 70%×95%+N−1 policy used for the headline 32-host total. At the same policy, the 40 ms SLO pole gives ceil(523/(17×0.70×0.95))+1 = ceil(46.26)+1 = 48 hosts, not 31. The chapter compares a full-util 40 ms screen to a policy 25 ms total.
evidence: 40 ms pole: W≈13.1 s, in-flight≈523. N_min=ceil(523/(17×0.70×0.95))=ceil(46.26)=47; +1 spare=48. 25 ms pole: 344/(17×0.70×0.95)=30.43→31; +1=32. The 31 and 32 are not comparable operating points.
root_cause: Denominator/operating-point mismatch: full-utilization screen vs policy screen; the 25 ms internal target and 40 ms SLO pole are not reconciled under one provisioning policy.
correction: Either size at the 40 ms SLO pole under the same u, ρ, and N_spare policy and report ~48 hosts, or explicitly state that 25 ms is the binding internal target and that 31 is a full-util screen not comparable to the 32-host policy total. Do not present 31 as the SLO-pole fleet size.
acceptance_test: Both poles are recomputed at identical u, ρ, and N_spare; the text states one sizing pole and all host counts use it; no apples-to-oranges comparison remains.

quoted_clause: W_e2e ... ≈ 10 s planning round (Ch 4: retrieval ~0.12 s + prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s, rounded)
observed: The listed components sum to 0.12+1.08+7.5=8.70 s, not ≈10 s. The table and later prose use W_e2e≈10 s, leaving a 1.3 s unexplained gap.
evidence: 0.12+1.08+7.5=8.70. Rounding 8.7 to one significant figure gives 9, not 10. If queue/tool/orchestration time is included, it is not named in the decomposition.
root_cause: Numerical inconsistency / missing component in the W_e2e decomposition.
correction: Change W_e2e to ≈8.7 s, or add and name the missing ~1.3 s (queue/tool/orchestration) and update all references. Keep W_GPU-exec=8.6 s and W_e2e distinct.
acceptance_test: The sum of named components equals the stated W_e2e within rounding; all W_e2e references use the same value.

quoted_clause: If user sessions must maintain conversation state (KV cache, accumulated tool outputs, retrieval context), the load balancer must route subsequent requests from the same user to the same host (sticky sessions).
observed: Conversation state can be externalized (shared KV/prefix cache, session store, state transfer) and rehydrated on any host. Sticky sessions are one implementation choice, not a requirement. The word 'must' overstates and can lead to an unnecessary affinity architecture.
evidence: The text itself later contrasts stateless routing; stateful serving systems can use external caches or disaggregated state. Affinity is not logically necessary.
root_cause: Mechanism/implementation conflation: session state with host affinity.
correction: Replace 'must' with 'may require affinity unless state is externalized or shared'; describe sticky sessions as one option with trade-offs.
acceptance_test: The text no longer asserts affinity is mandatory and names at least one externalized-state alternative.

quoted_clause: The architect must choose between density (sticky sessions, higher per-host utilization) and evenness (stateless routing, lower per-host utilization but better load balance).
observed: Sticky sessions can improve KV/cache locality and effective density, but they can also cause skew: a popular user pins one host to capacity while others are underutilized, lowering system-wide utilization. The phrase 'higher per-host utilization' is ambiguous and can be read as higher system utilization, which is not generally true.
evidence: The preceding sentence says sticky sessions 'limit effective parallelism' because a popular user can pin a single host while others stand underutilized. That is lower system utilization, not higher.
root_cause: Ambiguous/contradictory trade-off label; conflates cache locality with utilization.
correction: Distinguish 'cache locality / KV reuse' from 'load balance.' Say sticky sessions can increase per-host cache hit rate and reduce recomputation, but risk skew and lower fleet utilization; stateless routing improves balance at the cost of lost locality.
acceptance_test: The text no longer claims sticky sessions generally yield higher per-host utilization; the trade-off is stated as locality vs balance with skew risk.

quoted_clause: serving all 12,000 output tok/s on one host needs 12,000 × (140/17 + 24.1) GB/token ≈ 388 TB/s
observed: The calculation fixes B=17 (KV capacity) while assuming 12,000 output tok/s. At B=17 and ~21 ms/step, the maximum output rate is 17/0.021≈810 tok/s, not 12,000. To serve 12,000 tok/s, the batch would be ~252 at 21 ms/step (or 344 at 8.6 s service), and the weight amortization would be 140/252 or 140/344, not 140/17. The 388 TB/s figure mixes incompatible operating points.
evidence: 17 tokens/step ÷ 0.021 s = 809.5 tok/s. 12,000/809.5≈14.8 hosts. At B=344, per-token bytes=140/344+24.1≈24.51 GB; ×12,000≈294 TB/s, still >26.8 TB/s but not 388 TB/s.
root_cause: Operating-point inconsistency: batch size and throughput are not tied by step time.
correction: Replace with a consistent calculation: at B=17, max output rate≈810 tok/s, so 12,000 tok/s needs≈15 hosts; or compute bandwidth at the actual batch implied by 12,000 tok/s and the step time. Remove or relabel 388 TB/s as a hypothetical.
acceptance_test: The calculation uses one consistent B, step time, and throughput; max output rate and host count reconcile.

quoted_clause: so 2.0 req/s/host is not simultaneously sustainable with decode. The 21/31/32 host counts derived from that rate are the KV screen's counts, unchanged. Under case(i) the prefill leg leaves ~7% headroom and does not bind against the 21-host KV screen
observed: The prefill check only shows prefill consumes ~93% of the idealized prefill ceiling under case(i); it does not compute decode's compute/bandwidth demand or show that the remaining ~7% is insufficient. The next sentence says case(i) 'does not bind,' which contradicts 'not simultaneously sustainable.' The claim is asserted, not derived.
evidence: A simultaneous feasibility check requires comparing both prefill and decode demand to the same resource budget. The text provides only prefill demand and prefill ceiling; decode demand is not quantified in this check.
root_cause: Incomplete conservation/feasibility check; conclusion outruns evidence.
correction: Either perform the decode resource check at 2 req/s and show the combined demand exceeds capacity, or soften to 'prefill alone leaves little headroom; simultaneous decode feasibility is not established by this screen.' Make the case(i) treatment consistent.
acceptance_test: The text either includes a decode demand calculation that supports non-sustainability, or no longer asserts non-sustainability; the case(i) 'does not bind' and 'not sustainable' statements are reconciled.

quoted_clause: The two readings agree on the base case: moving 5 MB at the fabric's own 1.25 GB/s takes t_transfer = 5 MB ÷ 1.25 GB/s = 4 ms, comfortably inside the 20 ms observed duration
observed: The two readings are 250 MB/s effective goodput and 1.25 GB/s instantaneous link rate — a 5× difference. They do not 'agree'; they both show the base case is benign. The phrase can mislead readers into thinking the effective and instantaneous rates are equal.
evidence: 1.25 GB/s ÷ 250 MB/s = 5. The text itself says the per-request goodput sits ~5× under the link rate.
root_cause: Imprecise wording; conflates 'both pass the check' with 'the values agree.'
correction: Replace 'agree' with 'both show the base case is benign' or 'the transfer fits within the observed duration.'
acceptance_test: The wording no longer implies the two rates are equal and distinguishes effective goodput from instantaneous link rate.

quoted_clause: A host may hold 17.5 KV-resident requests but never serve 17.5 at the quoted service time
observed: 17.5 is a concurrency (requests), not a rate. The sentence likely means 'serve 17.5 requests per second' or 'complete 17.5 requests per service time.' As written, it is dimensionally ambiguous.
evidence: C is in requests; C/W is in requests/s. The sentence mixes them.
root_cause: Unit/quantity ambiguity.
correction: Say 'hold 17.5 KV-resident requests but never sustain 17.5 request completions per second at the quoted service time' or 'never serve 17.5 concurrent requests at the quoted per-request latency.'
acceptance_test: The sentence states units explicitly and matches C vs C/W.

quoted_clause: per decode step the weights are read once (~14 GB) and B tokens are produced, so the per-GPU decode token rate ≈ B × HBM_BW ÷ weight_bytes, capped by compute and KV — at batch 1 that is ~239 tok/s per GPU ... at batch 100 ~23,900 tok/s per GPU
observed: The bandwidth formula counts only weight bytes. At the stated 600-token context and a 7B model, KV traffic is material: κ ≈ 0.524 MB/token, so batch 100 reads ≈31.4 GB of KV per decode step in addition to ≈14 GB of weights.
evidence: With HBM_BW ≈3.35 TB/s, the stated formula gives 3.35e12/14e9 ≈239 steps/s at B=1 and 100×239 ≈23,900 tok/s at B=100. Including KV gives 3.35e12/(14e9+100×600×0.524e6) ≈73.8 steps/s, or ≈7,380 tok/s at B=100, about 3.2× lower.
root_cause: Decode bandwidth model omits KV-cache read traffic; 'capped by compute and KV' is treated as a capacity check rather than a bandwidth term.
correction: Use denominator weight_bytes + B×context×κ (plus other per-step traffic) for the bandwidth-bound decode rate, or explicitly state the context/batch regime where KV traffic is negligible; recompute the 200-rps host count.
acceptance_test: At B=100, context=600, κ≈0.524 MB/token, HBM_BW≈3.35 TB/s, the printed per-GPU token rate is ≤≈7.4k tok/s, and the host-count derivation uses that rate.

quoted_clause: under 100% prefix reuse only the final call's new context is prefilled — 11,600 tokens, i.e. 2,400 new tokens (3 × 800 of retrieved context) once the 9,200-token prefix is served from cache; the 195 generated γ tokens are not prefilled — giving W(3) ≈ 14.14 s
observed: The arithmetic uses 11,600 prefill tokens, not 2,400. 14.14 s = (11,600/9,200)×1.08 + 0.025×495 + 3×0.133. Using the stated 2,400 new tokens gives ≈13.06 s.
evidence: Prefill term for 2,400 tokens: (2,400/9,200)×1.08 ≈0.282 s; decode 0.025×495 =12.375 s; tool 3×0.133 =0.399 s; total ≈13.06 s. The 14.14 s value is the no-prefix-reuse prefill of 11,600 tokens, not the 100%-reuse case.
root_cause: Conflates total final-call context (11,600 tokens excluding generated γ) with the new tokens that must be prefilled under 100% prefix reuse (2,400).
correction: Set W_reuse(3) ≈13.06 s using 2,400 new prefill tokens, or explain why the 9,200-token prefix is not actually reused; update Table 17-2 reuse rows, in-flight counts, N counts, and N−1 row.
acceptance_test: W_reuse(3) is recomputed as (2,400/9,200)×1.08 + 0.025×495 + 3×0.133 ≈13.06 s; all reuse-row in-flight and host counts in Table 17-2 and §17.8 are updated consistently.

quoted_clause: 6.24M requests/month × 9,500 tokens ≈ 5.93×10^10 tokens/month — giving ~$155,817 ÷ 5.93×10^10 ≈ $2.63/1M
observed: The canonical workload is stated as 10 rps average. At 10 rps over 30 days, monthly requests = 10×2,592,000 = 25.92M, not 6.24M. 6.24M/month implies ≈2.41 rps average.
evidence: 25.92M×9,500 = 2.4624×10^11 tokens/month; $155,817/2.4624×10^11 ≈ $0.633/1M, not $2.63/1M. The printed $2.63/1M and the 'close to $2.50' comparison depend on the 6.24M basis.
root_cause: Monthly volume basis is inconsistent with the canonical 10-rps average; the $/1M calculation and its comparison to the $2.50 FP16 row inherit the wrong denominator.
correction: Reconcile the volume basis: either use 25.92M requests/month for 10 rps average and recompute $/1M, or explicitly define 6.24M as a different average-rate scenario and stop calling it the canonical 10-rps workload.
acceptance_test: Monthly requests = average_rps×2.592×10^6; if average_rps=10, the text uses 25.92M and recomputes $/1M; if 6.24M is retained, the implied 2.41 rps is stated and the canonical 10-rps label is removed.

quoted_clause: 70B dense FP16 | 140 GB | — | — | 1 GPU | 1 ... 70B MoE FP16 (2/16 experts) | 140 GB | — | — | 1 GPU | 1
observed: A 140 GB weight footprint cannot fit on one 80 GB H100. The same row says the weights are spread across the 8-GPU pool under TP, so 'GPUs per instance = 1 GPU' contradicts both the VRAM and the parenthetical.
evidence: 140 GB > 80 GB; minimum single-instance placement without KV is ceil(140/80)=2 GPUs, and the canonical 436 GB KV budget requires the full 8-GPU pool. The MoE FP16 row has the same 140 GB footprint and the same error.
root_cause: The 'GPUs per instance' column was filled with the number of instances or a nominal model count rather than the minimum device count required by the stated VRAM.
correction: Change the 70B dense FP16 and 70B MoE FP16 rows to 8 GPUs per instance for the canonical KV profile (or 2 GPUs minimum without KV), and make the 'instances on one 8×H100 pool' column consistent with that placement.
acceptance_test: For every row, GPUs_per_instance×80 GB ≥ weights + KV for the stated profile; the 70B FP16 and MoE FP16 rows no longer claim 1 GPU for 140 GB.

quoted_clause: The canonical case is *one* regime — a mid-context, mid-rate RAG workload where the KV-residency ceiling happens to be the binding constraint. ... Under case (ii) the prefill screen — not the KV screen — sets the 40-rps capacity floor (34 vs 32).
observed: The first sentence says the canonical case is KV-bound; the Table 17-2 note says under case (ii) the prefill screen sets the 40-rps floor (34 vs 32). Both cannot be true for the same canonical case without qualification.
evidence: Table 17-2 gives KV-only 32 total at 40 rps and case (ii) prefill 34 total; the note explicitly says prefill, not KV, sets the floor under case (ii). The counter-scenario lesson also repeats 'canonical regime ... KV-bound'.
root_cause: The canonical case is described as KV-bound without naming the prefill case; the later case (ii) screen contradicts the unqualified claim.
correction: Qualify the canonical claim: KV is the binding term among the KV/bandwidth screens, but the full-square prefill screen can bind under case (ii); state which case is being used whenever 'KV-bound' is asserted.
acceptance_test: Every canonical 'KV-bound' statement names the prefill case or is changed to 'KV-bound under case (iii)/KV-only screen'; the Table 17-2 note and the counter-scenario lesson agree.

quoted_clause: That is ~350 GB of weights, leaving ~290 GB of VRAM after weights — 226 GB of KV once the ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve is subtracted (640 − 350 − 64; the figure used below, C = floor(226/24.89) = 9)
observed: The calculation treats 8×H100 as one 640 GB pool. The 70B FP16 tier is tensor-parallel across all 8 GPUs; the 8-bit tiers need 2 GPUs each; the 4-bit copies need 1 GPU each. Aggregate free memory does not guarantee per-GPU free memory or a feasible TP placement.
evidence: A plausible placement leaves some GPUs with ≈27.5 GB free and others with ≈62.5 GB free before reserve. The FP16 tier's per-request KV is sharded across all 8 GPUs (≈3.11 GB/GPU per canonical request), so the minimum-free GPU, not the 226 GB sum, bounds C. The stated C=9 may not be achievable.
root_cause: Aggregate VRAM arithmetic ignores per-GPU capacity, TP group boundaries, and placement constraints.
correction: Show a per-GPU memory ledger for the co-resident placement and compute C from the minimum free memory in the TP group (or use a placement solver); if C=9 is not feasible, reduce it and update the fleet arithmetic.
acceptance_test: A per-GPU table lists weights, reserve, and free memory for each of the 8 GPUs; C is derived from the minimum free per-GPU memory times TP size divided by per-request KV, and the co-residency claim is accepted only if every GPU stays within 80 GB.

quoted_clause: 226 GB of KV once the ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve is subtracted ... — for KV cache and for smaller specialized models (e.g., 22B, 8B) for classification or routing
observed: The same 226 GB is then fully consumed by C = floor(226/24.89) = 9 canonical requests. No capacity remains for the smaller specialized models the sentence says the 226 GB is also for.
evidence: 9×24.89 GB = 224.0 GB, leaving ≈2 GB of the 226 GB, not enough for a 22B or 8B model at any useful precision. The sentence and the C calculation use the same budget for different purposes.
root_cause: The KV budget and the smaller-model budget are not separated; the prose implies both share 226 GB while the arithmetic assigns all of it to KV.
correction: Either state that C=9 is the KV-only capacity before smaller models and reduce C by the smaller-model weights, or allocate a separate VRAM line for the smaller models and recompute C.
acceptance_test: The sum of KV for C requests + smaller-model weights + reserve ≤640 GB, and the text states the same C after the smaller-model allocation.

quoted_clause: which minimizes weighted cost = α·token_cost + β·latency_cost?
observed: token_cost is USD per 1M tokens and latency_cost is USD per ms (or a normalized score). The table's formula adds quantities with different units; the following note says the gate must be evaluated in a per-request additive form or after normalization.
evidence: The note itself states 'different units, so the gate is evaluated in the per-request additive form cost = α·rate_tok·n_tok + β·rate_ms·n_ms ... or equivalently by normalizing both terms to [0,1]'. The table formula is dimensionally invalid as printed.
root_cause: The table was not updated when the units note was added; it still shows the pre-normalization shorthand as if it were the decision formula.
correction: Replace the table formula with the per-request additive form or with normalized scores, and make the table match the note and §18.3.4.
acceptance_test: Table 18-1's formula has consistent units and is identical in form to the units note; a reader can substitute the §18.3.2 rates without an implicit normalization step.

quoted_clause: 70B 4-bit GGUF | — | — | ~35 GB | 1 GPU ... 70B 4-bit GGUF local, no GPU
observed: The hardware table gives the 70B 4-bit GGUF row 1 GPU and counts GPU-resident copies, while the row-hardware note says the same tier is 'local, no GPU'. The $0.15/1M rate is 'energy only' and is not comparable to the GPU-resident copies.
evidence: The table's last column says '~18 by weights alone; ~5 if the 436 GB canonical KV budget is reserved ... worked deployment reserves 2', which is a GPU-memory calculation. The row-hardware note says 'local, no GPU'. These describe different deployments under one row label.
root_cause: The CPU/edge GGUF tier and the GPU-resident 4-bit fallback copies are conflated in one table row and one price row.
correction: Split the 4-bit GGUF row into (a) CPU/edge local, no GPU, energy-only and (b) GPU-resident 4-bit copies with capital+energy; or relabel the table row and price basis to the GPU-resident deployment and move the local tier to a separate row.
acceptance_test: The 4-bit GGUF row's GPU count, instance count, and price basis all describe the same deployment; the 'local, no GPU' tier is not used to justify a GPU-resident copy count.

quoted_clause: one host here serves the model on one GPU, so the per-host rate is the per-GPU rate above
observed: The book's canonical host is 8×H100. Earlier in the same paragraph the text says the 7B model runs on one GPU and '×8 if data-parallel replicated'. If a host has 8 GPUs, a host can serve up to 8 independent 7B replicas, so the per-host rate is not the per-GPU rate.
evidence: The base hardware is stated as 8×H100, 640 GB total VRAM. The phrase 'one host here serves the model on one GPU' silently changes the host definition to a 1-GPU host, which is inconsistent with the rest of the book.
root_cause: Host and GPU are conflated in the counter-scenario; the per-host rate is computed on a 1-GPU host while the canonical host is 8 GPUs.
correction: Either state explicitly that this counter-scenario uses a 1-GPU host, or multiply the per-GPU rate by the number of replicas per 8×H100 host (up to 8) and recompute the host count.
acceptance_test: The counter-scenario's host definition matches the book's 8×H100 host, or the text explicitly labels it a 1-GPU host and uses that definition consistently in the host-count formula.

quoted_clause: derive per-host concurrent capacity C from the *canonical* per-token KV (2 × layers × hidden × bytes)
observed: The formula 2×layers×hidden×bytes is the full-MHA KV size per token. For GQA/MQA, the KV dimension is n_kv_heads×head_dim, not hidden. The same lesson lists GQA/MQA as a capacity lever, so the checklist formula does not transfer to the lever it recommends.
evidence: For full MHA, hidden = n_heads×head_dim and the formula is correct. For GQA/MQA, n_kv_heads < n_heads, so using hidden overstates KV by n_heads/n_kv_heads. The canonical 70B full-MHA reference is a special case, not the general formula.
root_cause: The canonical full-MHA formula is presented as the general per-token KV formula in the architect's checklist.
correction: Write the general form as 2×layers×n_kv_heads×head_dim×bytes, note that full MHA sets n_kv_heads=n_heads, and use the canonical 2×layers×hidden×bytes only for the full-MHA reference.
acceptance_test: The checklist formula reduces to the canonical 2.62 MB/token for the 70B full-MHA reference and to a smaller value for GQA/MQA; the GQA/MQA lever is not evaluated with the full-MHA formula.

quoted_clause: 70 GB weights + 24.9 GB FP16 KV = 94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU
observed: 94.9 GB is the per-instance total, not a per-GPU quantity. With 2 GPUs per instance, the per-GPU share is ≈47.45 GB, which is below 80 GB. The comparison as written is dimensionally wrong even though the 2-GPU conclusion is correct.
evidence: The row says '2 GPU' and '94.9 GB > 80 GB per GPU'. The correct statement is '94.9 GB > 80 GB single-GPU capacity, so 2 GPUs are required'; the per-GPU load after sharding is 47.45 GB.
root_cause: Total instance memory is compared to per-GPU capacity without dividing by the number of GPUs.
correction: Rewrite as '94.9 GB total > 80 GB single-GPU capacity; with 2 GPUs the per-GPU share is ≈47.45 GB' and apply the same wording to the MoE 8-bit row.
acceptance_test: The row's inequality uses consistent units: total instance bytes vs total capacity of the stated GPU count, or per-GPU bytes vs 80 GB.

quoted_clause: priced on two bases (self-amortized capital+energy, energy-only) ... 70B dense FP16 | $2.50 | 120 | capital + energy
observed: The note says there are two bases: self-amortized capital+energy and energy-only. The FP16 row's basis is 'capital + energy', which is not one of the two named bases. If it is the same as self-amortized, the label should match; if it is a third basis, the note is wrong.
evidence: The table's other capital rows say 'self-amortized capital + energy'; the FP16 row says 'capital + energy'. The basis note's two-basis taxonomy does not include the latter label.
root_cause: Basis labels drifted between the table and the note.
correction: Unify the FP16 row to 'self-amortized capital + energy' if that is the intended basis, or add the third basis to the note and explain how it differs.
acceptance_test: Every row's Basis entry is one of the bases named in the note, and the note's count of bases matches the table.

quoted_clause: Σ per-call input across the task is 23,927 tokens/request — §8 ledger — and that is the token count the cost model uses.
observed: 23,927 is the ledger's total token count including outputs (2,392,670/100), not Σ per-call input. The ledger's expected input is 23,536.35 tokens/request; expected output is 390.35; total 23,926.7.
root_cause: The summary conflates total tokens with input tokens; the cost formula needs separate input and output quantities.
correction: Replace with 'Σ per-call input is ≈23,536 tokens/request and Σ output is ≈390 tokens/request; total processed tokens ≈23,927/request.' Ensure the cost model uses input and output separately.
acceptance_test: Recompute the ledger's input and output sums independently; the cost model must not use 23,927 as an input-token count.

page_hint: Ch 19 §8, 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger' table and following paragraph
quoted_clause: Peak KV residency follows the retained-context convention of §4 — 12,095 × 2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB at the completed T = 3 class.
observed: The table mixes bases: T=1 26.4 GB = 10,065×2.62 (input only), T=2 28.6 GB = 10,930×2.62 (input only), T=3 31.7 GB = 12,095×2.62 (input+300 output), fallback 30.9 GB = 11,795×2.62 (input only). The note only flags T=1 and fallback, not T=2.
root_cause: Two KV-residency conventions are used in one table; the explanatory note is incomplete.
correction: Choose one convention for all rows. If using final retained context incl terminal answer, print 27.2 / 29.4 / 31.7 / 30.9 GB (fallback no synthesis). If using input-only, print 26.4 / 28.6 / 30.9 / 30.9 GB. Update the note to cover every row.
acceptance_test: Every row's GB value must equal the declared token basis × 2.62 MB; no row may switch basis.

quoted_clause: A bottleneck in the tool backend will manifest as increased λ_tool, which directly inflates the per-turn loop overhead L_agent (§4), and through it the full service time W.
observed: This contradicts the earlier explicit separation: W's tool leg uses Chapter 17's ~133 ms/turn tool/retrieval rate, not L_agent's λ_tool≈100 ms; the text says the two are 'not additive' and 'different quantities.'
evidence: W(T) formula uses T·λ_tool/retr (≈133 ms/turn), while L_agent=λ_step+λ_tool≈220 ms/turn. An increase in λ_tool does not mechanically flow into W as defined.
root_cause: The paragraph collapses two distinct tool-latency quantities that the chapter elsewhere separates.
correction: Say the bottleneck inflates L_agent; if the W evaluator's tool/retrieval rate is also updated, W rises, but the mapping must be stated explicitly. Do not say 'through it' without qualification.
acceptance_test: Trace λ_tool into the W formula; show whether W uses λ_tool or λ_tool/retr, and keep the two rates distinct.

quoted_clause: The **incremental added latency** — the base generation plus the added orchestration overhead — is: L_orch(T) = L_base + T · L_agent
observed: L_orch(0)=L_base, so this is not incremental added latency; it is base-plus-orchestration total. The incremental added latency is T·L_agent.
evidence: At T=0, L_orch=8.6 s, which is the baseline, not an increment. The chapter later calls the same row 'Base + orchestration subtotal.'
root_cause: The label 'incremental added latency' is applied to a total that includes the baseline.
correction: Rename to 'orchestration-view total latency' or 'base + orchestration subtotal'; reserve 'incremental added latency' for T·L_agent. Update the following sentence that says it 'isolates how much the agentic layer's orchestration adds.'

quoted_clause: a fallback request attempts the full cap (T = 3 — 3 model calls + 3 tool calls) before the guardrail trips
observed: This conflicts with the earlier definition: 'A T-turn trace is T+1 model invocations.' A completed T=3 trace has four model invocations; the fallback has three attempted turns plus a single-shot re-dispatch and no terminal synthesis call.
evidence: Earlier: 'A T-turn trace is T+1 model invocations.' Fallback ledger inputs 9,200+10,065+10,930=30,195 for three attempted turns, then +9,200 single-shot; no 11,795 terminal synthesis call.
root_cause: The fallback's 'T=3' means three attempted agent turns, not a completed T=3 trace; the parenthetical uses the wrong call count.
correction: Write 'three attempted agent turns (3 model calls + 3 tool calls), with no terminal synthesis call' or otherwise distinguish attempted turns from completed T=3.
acceptance_test: Count model calls in the fallback trace; the description must match the ledger's 3 attempted + 1 single-shot calls.

quoted_clause: The guardrail budget caps total input at 13,000 tokens — a safety margin above the append-only worst case (12,660 at T = 4, Table 19-1), so the turn cap binds before the guardrail does.
observed: 'Total input' is ambiguous. If it means cumulative input across calls, T=1 already sums to 19,265 tokens, far above 13,000. The comparison to 12,660 only makes sense for per-call final context length.
evidence: Table 19-1's 12,660 is 'Retained-context input, final call'; the §8 ledger's T=1 Σ per-call input is 19,265.
root_cause: The guardrail is described as a total-input cap but compared to a per-call context length.
correction: Say 'caps per-call input context at 13,000 tokens' or 'caps the final-call context at 13,000 tokens'; if the guardrail is cumulative, recompute the binding point.
acceptance_test: State the guardrail's unit and interval; verify 13,000 against the same quantity (per-call vs cumulative).

evidence: The ledger's T=3 total is 42,485 =41,990 input +495 output. Table 19-1's final-call input is 11,795; 12,095 includes output.
root_cause: The term 'billable tokens' is used for billable input tokens, and the comparison quantity is mislabeled.

quoted_clause: The scheduling unit is the whole request, not the model call: the request holds its KV slot across every tool round-trip, so a T = 3 request occupies capacity for W ≈ 17.70 s even though the GPU is idle for the tool legs — concurrency is set by wall-clock occupancy, not by GPU-busy time.
observed: This is presented as a universal architecture consequence, but it depends on the stated no-reuse/hold-KV policy. Systems that offload, swap, or free KV during tool waits would not have concurrency set by full wall-clock occupancy.
evidence: The chapter's own policy says no prefix cache is reused and the request holds its KV slot; other serving designs can offload KV.
root_cause: A policy-dependent statement is written as a general law.
correction: Qualify: 'Under the stated hold-KV/no-reuse policy...' and note that KV offload/swap changes the occupancy calculation.
acceptance_test: Check whether the sentence is true under alternative KV-offload policies; if not, add the qualifier.

quoted_clause: Under this convention the 2% fallback is a high-tail/failure category that incurs zero added turns (single-shot)

evidence: The same section's ledger gives fallback added orchestration 660 ms + ~200 ms ≈860 ms and 39,395 input tokens.
root_cause: The qualifier 'for retained-context expectation' is dropped in the conditional paragraph.
